data.title: Wall Street slides as yields remain in focus ahead of the FOMC rate decision
data.description:
Wall Street’s major market averages declined Tuesday as Treasury yields remained the focal point and investors awaited the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision later this week.

The blue-chip Dow (DJI) was last -0.6%, the benchmark S&P 500 (SP500) was last -0.1%, and the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) was last -0.2%, 

From a sector-by-sector vantage point, nine of the 11 segments were in the red and were led lower by consumer staples. At the other end of the spectrum, energy was the strongest performer. 

The bond-market selloff adds pressure ahead of the Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision Wednesday, with investors expecting officials to raise short-term borrowing costs for the first time since July 2023.

The U.S. 2-Year Treasury yield (US2Y) inched down 1 basis point to 4.65%, the U.S. 10-Year Treasury yield (US10Y) ticked higher by 1 basis point to 5.00%, and the U.S. 30-Year Treasury yield (US30Y) pushed up 2 basis points to 5.37%. 

“The Federal Reserve has little choice but to hike rates on Wednesday, especially since the bond market has been signaling for weeks that higher rates are warranted, given warm inflation data, strong earnings and a sturdy labor market. The stock market would be disappointed if the Fed didn't hike rates on Wednesday,” Carol Schleif of BMO Wealth Management stated.

As for stocks that were on the move, shares of QUALCOMM (QCOM) +4.7%, while shares of Coinbase (COIN) fell -6.3%

data.title: Smith-Midland secures $2.2M contract for Newport News Navy Project
data.description:
Smith-Midland (SMID) on Tuesday announced that it has secured a $2.2M contract to manufacture and supply SlenderWall architectural precast panels, architectural precast components, and precast stair systems for a new operations and office facility at Newport News Shipbuilding in Newport News, Virginia.

Working with Hourigan Construction, Smith-Midland will manufacture the precast products at its Midland, Virginia, facility, with production scheduled to begin in October 2026 and installation expected to commence in November 2026.

The new facility will support U.S. Navy aircraft carrier inactivation programs, providing a dedicated operational headquarters and workspace for shipbuilders and naval personnel responsible for one of the nation's most critical defense missions, the company stated. 

Source: press release

data.title: Ecopetrol interim CEO Hurtado resigns, to be succeeded by Barco
data.description:
Ecopetrol (EC) said late Monday that interim CEO Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra has resigned, temporarily replaced by current Corporate VP of Finance and Sustainable Value Camilo Barco Muñoz; Vice Chairperson Hildebrando Velez also has resigned.

Barco Muñoz brings more than 35 years of senior executive experience in investment banking, corporate finance, and corporate governance in both the public and private sectors, with a particular focus on energy, the company said.

Ecopetrol (EC) Chairman Luis Felipe Henao sought Hurtado's resignation following a leaked audio recording, according to The Rio Times.

data.title: DoorDash partners with Wonder in major food tech tie-up
data.description:
DoorDash (DASH) announced a strategic partnership with Wonder that will include acquiring Wonder's Grubhub Campus Dining business. In addition, DoorDash (DASH) made a long-term investment in Wonder as part of its Series D round.

Grubhub Campus Dining, formerly known as Tapingo, allows students to order meals from campus dining facilities and on-campus restaurants using its mobile app or kiosks, pay for the meal with the convenience of campus dining dollars, and schedule the pickup. Grubhub Campus Dining is live at more than 450 colleges and universities, serving a significant portion of U.S. higher education students. 

Looking ahead, DoorDash (DASH) intends to continue expanding Grubhub Campus Dining in the U.S., enhance the selection and convenience available to students, and bring Tapingo’s vertically integrated technology stack beyond college campuses to stadiums, hotels, and other similar venues.

The transaction is anticipated to close by the first half of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory review.

Notably, DoorDash (DASH) made a $125M investment in Wonder to add to the company's $650M Series D round announced in July.

Wonder is Marc Lore’s food-tech company, designed as a “mealtime platform” rather than a conventional restaurant or delivery app. It operates food-hall-style locations where one shared kitchen produces dishes from many restaurant concepts, which range from Wonder-created brands to menus associated with chefs and established restaurants. Customers can combine items from multiple menus in one order for delivery, pickup, or dine-in.

Founded in 2018, Wonder originally used mobile kitchens that cooked near customers’ homes, then shifted toward physical locations supported by centralized preparation and local finishing kitchens. Its model is highly vertically integrated since Wonder controls its app, food production, and last-mile delivery.

data.title: Supply constraints are back and policymakers face a tougher economic trade-off
data.description:
The global economy has entered a new supply-driven regime in which shortages and constraints, rather than weak demand, are increasingly shaping growth and inflation, according to Deutsche Bank Research.

The shift marks a significant departure from the 2010s, when policymakers were primarily concerned about deficient demand, low inflation and persistently weak interest rates.

Deutsche Bank strategist Henry Allen said the return of supply-side constraints is making much of the previous decade’s economic playbook less effective, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in 2026 providing the latest example of how supply disruptions can affect oil prices, inflation and growth.

The transition became apparent during the Covid-19 pandemic, when unprecedented fiscal and monetary stimulus collided with disrupted supply chains and a sharp shift in consumer spending toward goods.

Shipping bottlenecks, labor-market disruptions and reduced energy investment compounded the mismatch between demand and supply. Inflation subsequently surged, with U.S. CPI reaching 7% in December 2021 before the Russia-Ukraine war delivered another major energy and food shock. U.S.

CPI eventually peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, while Eurozone inflation reached 10.6% in October 2022, prompting the Federal Reserve to raise rates by 525 basis points and the European Central Bank by 450 basis points during 2022-23, Deutsche Bank noted.

Supply pressures have persisted through subsequent years, from Red Sea shipping disruptions and Panama Canal drought conditions to industrial policy, tariffs and geopolitical fragmentation.

Deutsche Bank highlighted the latest closure of the Strait of Hormuz as another major supply shock, noting that roughly 25% of global seaborne oil trade previously passed through the waterway.

With limited traffic still able to pass, Brent crude has moved back above $100 a barrel and European natural gas prices have risen to their highest levels since late 2022. The report said these developments reinforce the view that supply shocks, rather than demand weakness, are increasingly responsible for major economic disruptions.

The new regime creates three major challenges for policymakers, according to Deutsche Bank. First, inflation spikes could become more frequent because economies have less spare capacity to absorb unexpected increases in demand.

Aging populations, shrinking working-age populations, reshoring efforts and higher defense spending are all limiting productive capacity. Second, monetary policy is less effective against supply shocks because interest-rate cuts can stimulate demand but cannot directly restore lost production capacity.

Third, fiscal stimulus is more likely to generate overheating and crowd out private investment, particularly as government borrowing costs have risen from the unusually low levels seen after the global financial crisis.

Deutsche Bank said the experience of the 1970s offers an important, though imperfect, precedent. Repeated oil shocks helped produce a stagflationary environment in which inflation rose while growth slowed, demonstrating how successive supply disruptions can become cumulatively damaging and potentially destabilize inflation expectations.

The longer-term response, however, can also strengthen economic resilience: the oil shocks ultimately encouraged the U.S. to build strategic reserves, increase domestic energy production and reduce its dependence on Middle Eastern oil.

Similarly, today's supply constraints could accelerate investment in energy, housing, labor-force participation and more resilient supply chains.

The report concludes that the central policy challenge has shifted from stimulating demand to expanding the economy's productive frontier and allowing growth to increase without generating persistent inflation.

data.title: Disorderly yield spike is now the market’s biggest tail risk, BofA highlights
data.description:
Fund managers have shifted their primary market worry. Bank of America’s September Global Fund Manager Survey, which polled 170 investors overseeing $470B in assets now ranks a disorderly rise in bond yields as the top tail risk.

A total of 33% of the respondents cited yields as the top tail risk. That reading is up from 27% in August and knocks last month’s leader—an AI bubble—down to 28% from 32%.

The change marks the first time this year that yield instability has outranked AI concerns in the monthly poll. A second wave of inflation still registered with 24% of managers. Geopolitical conflict, a Democratic sweep in the U.S. midterms, and dollar debasement trailed far behind at 6%, 5%, and 2%, respectively. 

The reordering of risks arrives as global yields have climbed to multiyear highs, with the U.S. 10-Year Treasury yield (US10Y) recently pushing above 5%.

BofA’s long-running survey treats tail risks as low-probability events with outsized impact. The latest results suggest institutions are more focused on a sudden repricing of duration than on a collapse in the AI trade—even as crowded semiconductor positioning remains a separate, closely watched theme.

data.title: Eli Lilly boosted to Buy at Berenberg as upside to 2026 guidance seen
data.description:
Berenberg upgraded Eli Lilly (LLY) to Buy from Hold, saying that it sees the drugmaker exceeding its 2026 guidance driven by continuing its lead in the weight-loss drugs market.

The firm upped its price target to $1400 from $1220 (~23% upside based on Sept. 14 close).

Analyst Kerry Holford said that Zepbound and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) are, respectively, the market leaders in obesity and diabetes. And while weight-loss pill Foundayo (orforglipron), which launched in April, has had a slow uptake, "we expect the imminent diabetes approval for Foundayo (oral GLP-1) to unlock significant demand."

She added that the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, which provides eligible Medicare Part D enrollees access to certain GLP-1 meds for $50 a month, "is fueling a steep uptick in Lilly's obesity drug demand." 

Holford noted that the company's strong pipeline has been bolstered by the acquisition of psychedelic-focused treatment developer AtaiBeckley for mental health disorders and Centessa for sleep-wake disorders.  

"Year to date, Lilly has committed cUSD60bn on more than 25 business development deals, with plenty of capacity to spend more," she wrote. "Many of the resulting new pipeline entrants have multibillion-dollar sales potential and offer important diversification optionality."

data.title: Most fund managers see little yield impact from Treasury buybacks
data.description:
Nearly half of global fund managers expect the U.S. Treasury's bond buyback program to have no impact on Treasury yields, while fewer see the program pushing yields higher, according to BofA Global Research.

The BofA Global Fund Manager Survey showed 46% of investors expected no impact on U.S. Treasury yields from the buyback program, while 29% expected the program to fail and yields to rise. Another 16% expected a successful program to result in a decline in Treasury yields.

The survey covered the Treasury's decision to double the size of its bond buybacks from Sept. 9 to Nov. 4, with respondents asked about the most probable outcome of the program.

The results show investors were largely unconvinced that the buyback program would materially change the direction of Treasury yields, with the largest share of respondents seeing no impact.
